title: xBind: an integrated webserver for large language model-enabled cross-molecular protein binding site prediction.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: The paper itself ships no data (its data availability statement is only the webserver address), so I downloaded the eight benchmark sets it is evaluated on from the third-party repositories named in the supplement: GraphPPIS (Train_335, Test_60, Test_315, UBtest_31), GraphSite (DNA_Train_573, DNA_Test_129, DNA_Test_181) and GraphBind (RNA-495_Train, RNA-117_Test, 287 KB zip). All parsed first try: each record is a header (PDB identifier plus chain), the amino-acid sequence, and a same-length string of 0/1 marking non-binding/binding for that residue. I counted: 2,236 unique chains, 598,395 labelled residues, 59,212 binding. Every one of the eight rows of Supplementary Table S1 reproduced exactly (e.g. Train_335 = 335 chains / 10,374 binding / 55,992 non-binding; DNA_Test_181 = 181 / 3,208 / 72,050; RNA-117_Test = 117 / 2,031 / 35,314). Zero length mismatches between sequence and label string, zero exact duplicate chain identifiers, label alphabet only {0,1}, 20 standard amino acids. I also measured that GraphBind's two alternative annotations for the same training chains (homology-transferred versus directly observed) disagree on 3,405 of 159,883 DNA residues and 2,853 of 136,899 RNA residues (about 2.1%). I checked the EquiPPIS and EquiPNAS GitHub repositories (both GPL-3.0, code plus example inputs present, trained weights on Zenodo).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The definition of a binding residue (a surface residue losing more than 1.0 square angstrom of absolute solvent accessibility when the complex forms), the network architecture and training recipe, the AlphaFold2-predicted-structure benchmarking protocol, and the reported ROC-AUC/PR-AUC numbers. I did not run the xBind webserver or the EquiPPIS/EquiPNAS models, and did not download the Zenodo feature archives or AlphaFold2 structures.

a1_downloadable.note: Checked in the files: the paper gives only a webserver link, but all eight benchmark sets download without login from GraphPPIS/GraphSite GitHub and the GraphBind site, about 0.9 MB of text in total.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Checked in the files: each record carries a 0/1 string the same length as the sequence, one character per residue, so the label needs no construction.

a3_inputs_present.note: Checked in the files: full amino-acid sequences are in the records; no accession lookups needed. 3D structures would have to be fetched or predicted, but are optional for a sequence-only baseline.

a4_units_stated.note: Label is a binary class, not a measurement; its definition (loss of solvent accessibility on complex formation, BioLiP annotation for nucleic-acid sets) is stated in the supplement and on the GraphBind dataset page.

a5_enough_rows.note: Counted in the files: 598,395 labelled residues (59,212 binding) over 2,236 protein chains; chain-level n is 2,236, still far above the 1,500 threshold.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 0.9 MB of label text; about 1.5 GB for cached ESM-2 650M per-residue embeddings in half precision
a6_fits_laptop.note: Verified file sizes. The paper's own pipeline used ESM-2 15B on A40 GPUs, but a 650M-parameter sequence baseline fits 16 GB easily.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Strongest check here: all eight rows of Supplementary Table S1 reproduced to the exact residue from the downloaded files.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels come from experimentally solved complex structures in the PDB/BioLiP, not from a model. Caveat verified in the files: about 23% of nucleic-acid positives come from homology-based annotation transfer rather than direct observation (14,479 transferred versus 11,074 observed for DNA).

B1.why: Eight separate text files in two slightly different record formats; no joins needed, concatenates into one table.

B2.why: Parsed first try with 15 lines of Python; zero sequence/label length mismatches across all files.

B3.why: Same annotation idea throughout, but protein-protein sets use solvent-accessibility curation and nucleic-acid sets use BioLiP transfer.

B4.why: Verified: label alphabet is only {0,1}, no missing or qualitative values anywhere in the files.

B5.why: Verified: zero exact duplicate chain identifiers and zero duplicate sequences within each file.

B6.why: Record format and label semantics documented on the GraphBind dataset page and in the xBind supplement.

C1.why: Default project is beating published PR-AUC on these exact splits; only interesting if we win.

C2.why: Many open, reproducible models on these same splits with 30%-identity and release-date separation (see audit).

C3.why: Even the DNA-versus-RNA specificity angle is taken by DRNApred, GPSite and MPBind.

C4.why: Ground truth needs a co-crystal structure of the complex, which is slow and expensive to obtain.

C5.why: Published numbers on the identical split in the paper's Table 1, plus a trivial majority-class baseline.

D1.why: ESM-2, a protein language model with open downloadable weights, matches amino-acid sequence input exactly.

D2.why: Per-residue embeddings for 2,236 chains cache once on CPU; a linear or small head trains in minutes.

D3.why: ESM-2 is permissive, but the benchmark files carry no explicit licence and the paper is CC BY-NC (non-commercial).

E1.why: Files come pre-clustered at 30% sequence identity (CD-HIT) and split by PDB release date.

E2.why: Eight datasets, 2,236 chains; plenty of identity clusters and release years to hold out.

E3.why: Majority class is trivially computable; verified positive rate 4.3-15.8% depending on set.

E4.why: Measured it: transferred versus observed annotations disagree on about 2.1% of residues, giving an annotation noise floor.

E5.why: Arginine/lysine enrichment at nucleic-acid interfaces and surface exposure are textbook signals a working model must recover.

E6.why: Label shuffling and feature ablation are trivial on a 598,395-row residue table.

E7.why: DNA_Test_181 is a later-release set curated by a different group than DNA_Test_129; unbound set UBtest_31 adds a conformational check.

E8.why: EquiPPIS/EquiPNAS weights are on Zenodo under GPL-3.0 and GPSite/MPBind ship weights, but exact reproduction needs a GPU and AlphaFold2 models.

G1.why: Every record header is a PDB identifier plus chain, a standard joinable identifier; verified in the files.

G2.why: PDB, BioLiP2 and AlphaFold DB (via SIFTS chain-to-UniProt mapping) are all specific, joinable partners.

G3.why: PDB chain to UniProt is mostly clean but chimeric and multi-domain chains make some of it one-to-many.

G4.why: Proteome-scale annotation is the obvious combined question, and GPSite already did it for 568,000 sequences.

H1.why: Verified: 539,183 non-binding residues are labelled explicitly, not just the 59,212 positives.

H2.why: Many species and labs, but only proteins that crystallised in complex; disordered and membrane proteins are largely absent.

H3.why: Claim is statable in one sentence (see honest_claim_h3) because the inclusion criterion is explicit.

H4.why: Redundancy filtering, release-date split and annotation transfer are documented on the dataset page and in the supplement.

I1.why: Named users: the Bhattacharya lab (Virginia Tech), the biomed-AI group (Sun Yat-sen), and structural biologists planning interface mutagenesis.

I2.why: They already have working tools; another point of PR-AUC would not redirect an experiment.

I3.why: Field reports ROC-AUC/PR-AUC while the real decision is which handful of residues to mutate, which needs precision at top-k.

I4.why: Mapping sequence and structure context to interface residues is genuinely complex; simple charge rules fall well short.

J1.why: Per-residue classification with grouped splits, frozen-backbone transfer learning and class imbalance is real ML practice.

J2.why: Interface biochemistry is checkable by eye: basic residues at nucleic-acid interfaces, hydrophobic patches at protein interfaces.

J3.why: A unified cross-partner residue table is mildly shareable, but GPSite and MPBind already distribute equivalents.

J4.why: Scope is small enough to bound in two to three weeks, but no budget is written down anywhere.

J5.why: No kill date or condition recorded for this candidate.

existing_models.name: EquiPPIS (the protein-protein engine behind xBind, PLOS Computational Biology 2023)
existing_models.score_and_split: PR-AUC 0.4516 and ROC-AUC 0.7912 on Test_60 with AlphaFold2 structures, 30%-identity-filtered split; reported in this paper's Table 1
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Dependence on input structure quality and on costly evolutionary profiles; the paper frames unified cross-partner prediction in one tool as the remaining gap

existing_models.name: EquiPNAS (the protein-DNA/RNA engine behind xBind, Nucleic Acids Research 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: ROC-AUC 0.9159 on DNA Test_181 versus GraphSite 0.8964 and GraphBind 0.8916, 30%-identity and release-date split
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Generalisation to predicted rather than experimental structures, and reliance on 15-billion-parameter embeddings that are expensive to compute

existing_models.name: GPSite (eLife 2024), geometry-aware predictor of ten binding partner types
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported to surpass sequence- and structure-based methods on the same DNA/RNA/protein benchmarks; applied genome-wide to over 568,000 sequences
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Accuracy when predicted structures are poor, and coverage of rarer partner types

existing_models.name: MPBind (Bioinformatics 2025), multitask predictor over five partner classes
existing_models.score_and_split: ROC-AUC 0.83 protein-protein and 0.81 protein-DNA/RNA on its own held-out sets
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Transfer across partner classes with very unequal training data

existing_models.name: MegSite (2025), multimodal protein language model (ESM3) for nucleic-acid sites
existing_models.score_and_split: Matthews correlation 0.567 on DNA-129_Test and 0.444 on DNA-181_Test, the exact files I downloaded
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: RNA-binding sites remain harder than DNA; cross-type confusion persists

existing_models.name: DRNApred (Nucleic Acids Research 2017), sequence-based DNA- versus RNA-binding residue discriminator
existing_models.score_and_split: Cut cross-predictions by 26-43% (AURC/AULRC) against the then-second-best method on a DNA+RNA combined set
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Absolute accuracy of discrimination; it traded accuracy for specificity

existing_models.name: GraphPPIS, GraphBind, GraphSite, CLAPE-DB, PNABPred, PRIMED
existing_models.score_and_split: All report on Train_335/Test_60 or DNA_Train_573/Test_129/Test_181; e.g. PRIMED ROC-AUC 0.93 and Matthews correlation 0.45 on Test_129

backbone.name: ESM-2 (esm2_t33_650M_UR50D), a protein language model
backbone.hardware: 16 GB laptop CPU; about 1-2 hours to embed 2,236 chains once, then minutes per head
backbone.licence: MIT for ESM-2; benchmark files carry no stated licence and the paper is CC BY-NC

integration.partner_dataset: BioLiP2 and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, reached through the SIFTS PDB-chain-to-UniProt mapping
integration.join_key: PDB identifier plus chain, present in every record header, mapped to UniProt accession
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do interface predictors trained only on proteins that crystallised in complex transfer to the far larger set of proteins with only predicted structures - a question GPSite has already answered at the scale of 568,000 sequences.

controls.positive_control: The model must recover arginine/lysine enrichment and high solvent exposure at nucleic-acid interfaces, and must nail a trivial surrogate target such as residue hydrophobicity from the sequence.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the 0/1 label strings within each chain and confirm performance collapses to the 4-16% positive rate.
controls.external_validation: DNA_Test_181 (later PDB release dates, curated by a different group than Test_129) and UBtest_31 (unbound conformations of Test_60 proteins).

honest_claim_h3: Among single protein chains that were co-crystallised with a partner and deposited in the PDB before about 2021, the model ranks which surface residues contact a protein, DNA or RNA partner - it says nothing about disordered, membrane-embedded or never-crystallised proteins.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a protein's amino-acid sequence to predict which of its residues touch a protein, DNA or RNA partner.
plain_idea.train_on: One row per amino acid: the residue in its sequence context, optionally with structure-derived features. I counted 598,395 labelled residues across 2,236 protein chains in the eight downloaded benchmark sets.
plain_idea.predict: A 0/1 flag per residue saying whether it contacts the chosen partner type. The true answer comes from experimentally solved complex structures in the PDB, where a residue counts as binding if it loses solvent-accessible surface when the complex forms.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Structural biologists use these predictions to choose which residues to mutate when testing an interaction, but at least eight open models already do this job on these exact files, so the result would change nobody's practice.

more_or_better_data.why: There is no new data at all: the paper's data availability statement is only the webserver address, and the eight benchmark sets (2,236 chains, 598,395 residues) are 2018-2021 third-party files already used by EquiPPIS, EquiPNAS, GraphPPIS, GraphBind, GraphSite, GPSite, MPBind and MegSite.

confidence_score.why: The 2.1% disagreement I measured between transferred and directly observed annotations gives a per-residue label-reliability flag that published models ignore, but it is a small and uneven signal confined to the nucleic-acid training sets.

models_beatable.why: EquiPNAS (2024) and MegSite/PNABPred/PRIMED (2025-2026) are recent, use large protein language models, and are evaluated on 30%-identity-filtered sets split by PDB release date - an honest split, not a random one.

guaranteed_improvement.why: No new measurements join to these files; the same PDB-derived labels are all anyone has, so the only route is a better architecture on identical data, which guarantees nothing.

ml_idea: Freeze ESM-2 and fit a per-residue head to predict protein-, DNA- and RNA-binding residues on the eight benchmark splits that xBind reports on, using the 598,395 labelled residues I verified, and measure how much the structural features in EquiPPIS/EquiPNAS actually add over sequence alone, plus how often a DNA-trained head mislabels RNA-binding residues. Everything in that sentence - sequence-only language-model baselines, multitask cross-partner heads, and DNA-versus-RNA cross-prediction - has already been published by GPSite, MPBind and DRNApred on the same files.

effort.compute_note: Timed the download and parse (minutes, 0.9 MB of text, already done). Embedding and cross-validation times are estimates: 2,236 chains of median length about 200 residues at roughly 1-2 seconds per chain for ESM-2 650M on CPU, then a logistic or small multilayer head over 598,395 rows by 1,280 features.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count how many open models already report numbers on Test_60 / DNA_Test_129 / RNA-117_Test - I found at least eight, all with code or weights and 30%-identity plus release-date splits, which is the kill.

verdict_reason: Part A passes cleanly and the files are unusually tidy (all eight of Supplementary Table S1's rows reproduced exactly, 598,395 labelled residues, zero parse errors), but the paper contributes no data of its own - it is a web interface over two of its authors' earlier models - and residue-level binding-site prediction on these very files is one of the most saturated tasks in structural bioinformatics. At least eight open, reproducible models (EquiPPIS, EquiPNAS, GraphPPIS, GraphBind, GraphSite, GPSite, MPBind, PRIMED) already publish honest 30%-identity and release-date-split numbers on them, and the one residual angle, telling DNA- from RNA-binding residues apart, was taken by DRNApred in 2017 and by the multitask models since. C1, C2 and C3 all score 0: the only available result is a marginal gain against strong baselines.
